title: Learning the Language of a Trade
text:
Every profession develops a vocabulary that outsiders find opaque. Surgeons speak of 'anastomosis' without hesitation, while lawyers rely on 'estoppel' to close a line of argument. Such terms compress long explanations into single words, which makes communication efficient among specialists and mystifying to everyone else.

Mastering this language is less about memorising glossaries than about learning when a term is appropriate. A newcomer who uses jargon in the wrong setting may appear either pretentious or careless, whereas a skilled practitioner can translate fluently between the technical register and everyday speech. This flexibility, rather than the size of the vocabulary, is the true marker of expertise.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what do terms such as 'anastomosis' and 'estoppel' do?
options: Compress long explanations into single words
Are used only in written documents

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what can a newcomer who uses jargon in the wrong setting appear to be?
What does the passage suggest is the true marker of expertise?
options: The flexibility to move between technical and everyday registers

questions.text: Why does the passage describe jargon as efficient yet mystifying?
options: It is efficient for specialists but mystifying for outsiders
It is efficient only in writing
